extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, classicists, and advanced students/researchers studying Archimedes and the geometry of conics and surfaces
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and exposition of the geometric properties of plane sections of solids of revolution (conoids, spheroids, hyperboloids) as treated by Archimedes and his predecessors, and the arithmetic/notation practices used in related computations. Includes discussion of lemmas on surface-loci and classical Greek numeral/arithmetic methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections perpendicular to the axis are circles
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections made by planes perpendicular to the axis of revolution are circles (and not ellipses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes treats such perpendicular sections as circles and uses this fact to identify bases of segments whose volumes he later computes; the statement is presented as fundamental and 'manifest' in context of determining which sections may serve as circular or elliptic bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section of a spheroid by a plane parallel to the axis is an ellipse similar to the generating ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: A plane section of a spheroid (surface of revolution of an ellipse) by a plane parallel to the axis yields an ellipse similar to the generating ellipse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states this can be proved in the same way as the analogous theorem for the hyperboloid (case (2) earlier); Archimedes omits detailed proofs of such 'manifest' cases but they are asserted as readily deducible from conic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section of a hyperboloid by a plane parallel to the axis is a hyperbola similar to the generating hyperbola
rubrics_metrics.description: If a plane section is parallel to the axis of a hyperboloid of revolution, the section is a hyperbola similar to the original generating hyperbola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text outlines coordinate/proportional arguments showing y relates by a constant proportion as in the original hyperbola, establishing similarity; this is treated as a routine consequence of properties of central conics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section of a hyperboloid by a plane through the centre (vertex of enveloping cone) is a hyperbola (not necessarily similar)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plane through the centre (or the vertex of the enveloping cone) cutting a hyperboloid produces a hyperbola, but this hyperbola need not be similar to the generating hyperbola in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs are indicated by using the property that 'the rectangles under the segments of intersecting chords are as the squares of the parallel tangents' and then comparing proportional relations; the text also gives a geometric argument (drawing CC' etc.) to show non-similarity in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property of intersecting chords and tangents (used for proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rectangles under the segments of intersecting chords are as the squares of the parallel tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This classical property (enunciated as known from the 'elements of conics') is invoked as the principal tool Archimedes would have used to prove various section-theorems (e.g., Props. 3 and 12–14), rather than algebraic equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' preference: express central conics as proportions rather than equations between areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes expressed the equations of central conics in the form of a proportion (e.g. y^2:... = ...) and avoided expressing them as algebraic equations between areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that Archimedes' style favours proportions because expressing the conic relations as ratios between areas and lines would have been awkward and longer; thus proofs are geometrical and proportion-based rather than algebraic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'manifest' proofs and expectation of contemporaries' geometric familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes describes some section-theorems as 'manifest' — the text suggests this means easily deducible from known fundamental properties of conics and the fact that sections perpendicular to axes are circles, rather than necessarily citing prior proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used as an explanatory criterion for why Archimedes omits detailed proofs of several section-theorems: they are simple consequences of accepted conic properties and the definitions he uses, and so would have been considered obvious to contemporary geometers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pappus' first lemma on surface-loci (moving-conic description)
rubrics_metrics.description: If AB be a straight line and CD be parallel to a given straight line, and AD·DB : DC^2 is given, the point C' lies on a conic section; extending to the 3D case, moving AB with ends on given lines produces a surface-locus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text records Tannery's interpretation and discusses two special cases: (1) AB constant length with the two fixed lines parallel → a cylindrical surface (a conic moved bodily); (2) AB moves parallel to itself with fixed lines meeting → a cone. These interpretations give criteria for when a moving conic generates cylinders/cones and when Euclid might have considered such loci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pappus' second lemma: locus with distances in fixed ratio is a conic
rubrics_metrics.description: The locus of a point whose distance from a given point is in a given ratio to its distance from a fixed line (or plane) is a conic (ellipse/parabola/hyperbola according as the ratio is <, =, or > 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lemma is extended to 3D: taking planes perpendicular to a fixed line and intersecting a given plane yields a cone whose sections are the conics; further, treating distance from a point vs a plane gives the conoids and spheroids discussed by Archimedes. The text uses this to conjecture what Euclid's Surface-loci treatise might have contained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and assumed knowledge of constructions of two mean proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes assumes the construction of two mean proportionals (used in certain propositions of On the Sphere and Cylinder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He likely relied on classical constructions (Archytas, Menaechmus, Eudoxus); the text notes Archimedes only introduces geometric means where necessary and sometimes replaces them with arithmetic means when sufficient for his purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek numeral system conventions relevant to computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical Greek notation: letters denote 1–9, 10–90, 100–900; thousands are represented by the same letters with a mark; no zero sign; myriads (10,000) used as higher-order denomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This background is given as necessary context for interpreting numerical manipulations in Archimedes (Measurement of a Circle, Sand-reckoner). The lack of a zero and use of myriads affects how large numbers and place values were written and computed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexagesimal fractions and arithmetic methods (addition/multiplication/division)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greeks used sexagesimal fractional notation (degrees/minutes/seconds) for many computations; arithmetic procedures (addition, subtraction, multiplication, long division) were carried out in ways analogous to modern methods, keeping denominations separately and 'carrying' between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes practical methods: columnar organization of powers of 10 for addition/subtraction, decomposing the multiplier into powers for multiplication, and long-division procedures similar in spirit to modern long division. Examples from Eutocius, Heron, and Theon illustrate these procedures and their use in Archimedes' calculations.
